\chapter{Tuvieron --- the Strong Stems, Made Plural}
\label{ch:tuvieron}
\hlchaptermodality{202}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put the strong preterite stems into the plural.}

I can put the strong preterite stems into the plural.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tuvieron]{tuvieron}

\label{lesson:ES-C55-tuvieron}



\begin{quote}
Say the three strong pasts you know. (\emph{Tuve, hice, estuve}.) Where does the stress fall? (On the \textbf{stem} — \emph{TU-ve}, \emph{HI-ce}.)

That is what makes them strong. Now watch what the plural does to it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the stem gives the stress back}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Strong stem + \emph{-ieron}.}
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{singular} & \textbf{plural} \\
\midrule
\emph{tuve} & \textbf{tuvieron} \\
\emph{hice} & \textbf{hicieron} \\
\emph{estuve} & \textbf{estuvieron} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The ending is the same \emph{-ieron} you learned for \emph{comer} and \emph{vivir}. The strong stem does not change — \emph{tuv-}, \emph{hic-}, \emph{estuv-} — it simply takes the ordinary plural ending.

And the stress moves: \emph{TU-ve}, but \emph{tu-VIE-ron}. The stem holds it in \emph{tuve} and \emph{tuvo} and hands it back here, because \emph{-ieron} is two syllables and takes it.

Note that \emph{tuviste} never had it — \emph{tu-VIS-te} is stressed on the ending like any ordinary past. \textbf{The stem only ever held the stress in two of the forms}, which is exactly how much irregularity Spanish was willing to pay for.

No written accent on any of them — they end in \emph{-n}, so the default is already right, exactly as with \emph{hablaron}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tuve · tuvieron}
  \item \emph{hice · hicieron · estuvieron}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending do the strong stems take in the plural? (\textbf{-ieron} — the ordinary one.)

And what changes besides the ending? (The \textbf{stress}, back onto it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
